question: What is the main difference between geriatrics and gerontology?

options.B: Social interactions and community structures of aging populations
options.C: Cellular biology and genetic mapping of senescence
options.D: Medical care and treatment of diseases in older adults

explanation: Geriatrics focuses on the medical care and treatment of older adults, while gerontology looks at the broader aging process including social and biological aspects. [learn more](GNS321_U3_T2#GNS321_U3_T2_h1)

question: Why is it important for nurses to know the difference between normal aging and illness?

options.A: To lower the cost of pharmaceutical prescriptions
options.B: To eliminate the need for routine vital sign monitoring
options.C: To reduce hospital stay durations for administrative reports
options.D: To avoid inappropriate treatment or missed diagnoses

explanation: Recognizing normal body changes helps nurses avoid treating a healthy aging process as a disease or missing a real illness. [learn more](GNS321_U3_T2#GNS321_U3_T2_h1)

question: What common structural change happens to blood vessels as people age?

options.A: Loss of elastin and accumulation of collagen
options.B: Deposition of active skeletal muscle tissue
options.C: Enlargement of vascular smooth muscle lumen
options.D: Significant thinning of the tunica intima layer

explanation: Blood vessels stiffen over time because elastic fibers break down and collagen builds up in the artery walls. [learn more](GNS321_U3_T2#GNS321_U3_T2_h2)

question: An 80-year-old patient has stiffer chest walls. What breathing change is expected?

options.A: Rapid expansion of alveoli during quiet rest
options.B: Elevated arterial oxygen saturation levels at baseline
options.C: Reduced vital capacity and lower exercise tolerance
options.D: Increased total lung capacity and deep breathing ease

explanation: Stiffened chest walls limit full lung expansion, which reduces the amount of air a person can breathe in and out. [learn more](GNS321_U3_T2#GNS321_U3_T2_h2)

question: What is a main cause of ongoing constipation in older adults?

options.A: Excessive production of active gastric hydrochloric acid
options.C: Hypertrophy of the internal anal sphincter muscle
options.D: Rapid transit of stool through the large intestine

explanation: Slower bowel movements give the body more time to absorb water from stool, making it harder and more difficult to pass. [learn more](GNS321_U3_T2#GNS321_U3_T2_h3)

question: Why might a kidney blood test (serum creatinine) look normal in an older adult with failing kidneys?

options.A: Aging nephrons increase their filtration speed threefold
options.B: The liver compensates by excreting excess serum creatinine
options.C: Concurrent loss of muscle mass lowers creatinine production
options.D: Hydration status completely masks any functional nephron loss

explanation: Because older adults naturally have less muscle mass, their bodies produce less creatinine. This can keep blood test levels normal even when kidney function drops. [learn more](GNS321_U3_T2#GNS321_U3_T2_h3)

question: What term is used for the natural loss of muscle mass as people age?
explanation: Sarcopenia is the medical term for the gradual loss of muscle mass and strength that happens with aging. [learn more](GNS321_U3_T2#GNS321_U3_T2_h4)

question: Why are older adults more likely to get pressure sores?

options.A: Rapid regeneration of dermal collagen fibers
options.B: Loss of subcutaneous fat and decreased vascularity
options.C: Thickened epidermal layers blocking blood supply
options.D: Increased sweat gland production and skin moisture

explanation: Thinner skin with less padding and poorer blood flow makes it easier for pressure and friction to damage the tissue. [learn more](GNS321_U3_T2#GNS321_U3_T2_h4)

question: What is the medical term for age-related hearing loss?
explanation: Presbycusis refers to the gradual hearing loss that happens in both ears as a normal part of getting older. [learn more](GNS321_U3_T2#GNS321_U3_T2_h5)

question: A nurse is talking to an older patient who has trouble seeing and hearing. What should the nurse do?

options.A: Write all instructions in tiny font on standard paper
options.B: Dim the room lights to prevent eye strain and glare
options.C: Shout loudly from across the room using rapid speech
options.D: Face the patient directly and speak in a low, clear tone

explanation: Lower-pitched tones are easier to hear when someone has age-related hearing loss, and facing them helps them see your face clearly. [learn more](GNS321_U3_T2#GNS321_U3_T2_h5)

question: Which body change contributes to higher rates of type 2 diabetes in older adults?

options.A: Complete cessation of pancreatic insulin production
options.B: Accelerated destruction of alpha cells in the islets
options.C: Hypersecretion of thyroid hormones by the pituitary
options.D: Development of peripheral tissue insulin resistance

explanation: Over time, body cells become less responsive to insulin, which causes blood sugar levels to rise. [learn more](GNS321_U3_T2#GNS321_U3_T2_h6)

question: How does aging affect the immune system's response to infection?

options.A: It prevents chronic inflammatory disease development
options.B: It delays immune response and reduces vaccine effectiveness
options.C: It eliminates the need for standard infection control
options.D: It causes an immediate surge in white blood cell counts

explanation: An aging immune system reacts more slowly to new germs and does not build as strong a defense from vaccines. [learn more](GNS321_U3_T2#GNS321_U3_T2_h6)

question: Why might a low-grade fever be easily missed in an older adult?

options.A: Infection always causes body temperature to drop sharply
options.B: Elderly skin is too thick to register internal body heat
options.C: Thermometers cannot detect pathogens in older patients
options.D: Baseline normal body temperature is often lower in the elderly

explanation: Older adults often run lower baseline temperatures, meaning a slight rise may only look like a normal reading instead of a fever. [learn more](GNS321_U3_T2#GNS321_U3_T2_h7)

question: A doctor prescribes a standard adult dose of a drug cleared by the kidneys to an 85-year-old patient. What is the nurse's best action?

options.A: Administer the medication immediately as ordered by the doctor
options.B: Double the fluid intake to wash out the medication faster
options.C: Crush the tablet to speed up systemic drug absorption
options.D: Question the dosage due to reduced glomerular filtration and metabolism

explanation: Older kidneys clear drugs more slowly, which increases the risk of drug buildup and toxicity unless the dose is adjusted. [learn more](GNS321_U3_T2#GNS321_U3_T2_h7)
